title: Pilot study of Frunevetmab (Solensia) and Meloxicam for palliative therapy of feline bone-invasive oral squamous cell carcinomas
text:
Oral squamous cell carcinomas are a common oral cancer in cats. These tumors are locally aggressive and associated with tissue and 
bone destruction. The average survival time of cats with this oral tumor type is reported to be 3 months or less, even after
aggressive treatment. Many owners elect to pursue palliative (pain relief) care options rather than cancer treatments. However, 
there can be challenges with palliative care as the selection of pain medication for cats is limited and most require oral
administration. There is an unmet need for pain medications that are safe and effective at maintaining a good quality of life for
cats with oral tumors. Therefore, the goal of this study is to evaluate a currently available injectable drug, which is marketed for the treatment of arthritis pain in cats, for its ability to also provide relief of pain associated with oral cancers.

title: Radiotherapy Trial for Metastatic Bone Cancer in Dogs
text: Purpose of the study: This study seeks to determine whether a new treatment can be safe and effective to stop osteosarcoma or bone cancer that has spread or metastasized beyond the tumor in the limb.   Your pet will receive a small amount of a radiotherapy, which consists of a radioactive compound linked to a monoclonal antibody, called “225-Actinium 3F8 (225Ac-3F8) in a vein.  We will then do a  specialized type of imaging called Single Photo Emission Computed Tomography(SPECT) combined with a computed tomography (CT or CAT) scan to determine whether your pet’s tumor takes up this agent.  We will also take samples of blood, urine, and feces to try and determine the maximum dose that your dog can tolerate. We may then give an additional dose of 225Ac-3F8 in a vein several days later to treat your dog.  We will follow-up with sampling of the blood and another specialized imaging called Positron Emission Tomography-Computed Tomography (PET-CT) at approximately 40 days after treatment to determine your dog's response.

title: Combination chemotherapy (Doxorubicin-Temozolomide with or without propranolol) in dogs with Hemangiosarcoma
text: The objective of this study is to investigate the effectiveness of combining doxorubicin and temozolomide with or without propranolol in dogs with hemangiosarcoma. The use of either doxorubicin alone as a treatment for hemangiosarcoma has been studied, and studies with propranolol (historically used to treat heart disease) have shown promise as an added treatment against hemangiosarcoma, however, survival times still remain quite low. A sister drug to Temozolomide, DTIC, has shown promise in improving survival times, however side effects and the long administration times have created challenges with the use of DTIC in dogs. Temozolomide is administered orally and is historically well tolerated in dogs. We are hopeful that survival times can be further improved using a combination approach to treatment, with combination of both intravenous and oral treatments and improved tolerability. Dogs with hemangiosarcoma of the spleen, liver, heart or intramuscular region will be considered for inclusion in this study.

title: Embolization and Chemoembolization in dogs with non-resectable liver tumors
text: Embolization is a minimally invasive cancer treatment in which particles are used to block the blood supply to a tumor. For liver tumors, the particles are delivered to the tumor using a catheter (long, thin tube) placed into an artery in the neck or thigh and threaded through the blood vessel until it reaches the specific blood vessel providing blood to the tumor. This is called Trans-Arterial Embolization (TAE). In some cases, chemotherapy is delivered directly to the tumor through this catheter immediately prior to delivering the particles that block the blood vessel. This is called Trans-Arterial Chemoembolization (TACE). Both TAE and TACE are used to treat liver tumors in dogs, but it is unknown if adding chemotherapy to embolization (TACE) has any benefit over embolization alone (TAE). The first purpose of this study is to compare the outcomes of dogs receiving TAE to dogs receiving TACE. Both computed tomography (CT) angiograms and contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) are used to evaluate tumors in dogs. In people, CEUS has been shown to be more accurate than CT for assessing how effective the embolization procedure was in cutting off blood supply to the tumor. In dogs, a CT scan is the current standard for post-embolization evaluation. The second purpose of this study is to compare the accuracy of CEUS and CT scan following embolization.

title: Pilot Study for a New Quasiorganelle Therapy in Dogs with Histiocytic Sarcoma
text: Histiocytic sarcoma is an aggressive cancer in dogs that often does not respond well to standard treatments like chemotherapy or radiation. While some dogs experience benefits, these treatments affect many cells at once and cannot adapt as a tumor changes. New research shows that cancer closely interacts with the immune system and surrounding tissues, suggesting that better treatments may need to work inside cells, not just target them from the outside. Quasiorganelle therapy is an experimental approach that aims to do this by using weakened, non-disease-causing bacteria derived from Listeria monocytogenes to deliver helpful genetic instructions directly into immune and tumor cells, with the goal of improving how the body recognizes and responds to cancer.The first group (8 dogs) will receive quasiorganelle therapy alone. Their tumor will be measured and they will receive the quasiorganelle infusion. They will then be observed for up 4 days at the MSU Veterinary Medical Center and blood and fecal samples will be taken at set timepoints. The dogs will return for treatment once weekly for 4 doses followed by 2 weeks off. This schedule will then be repeated two more times for a total of 16 weeks of treatment. Imaging to determine alterations in tumor size will be repeated at the end of each 4 week treatment period.The second group (8 dogs) will receive quaisorganelle therapy that includes gene therapy. Their treatment and monitoring schedule will be identical to that of the first group.Following the 16 week treatment period, dogs will return for evaluation every 4 weeks or until progressive disease is documented.Please note: While enrolled, dogs should not live with anyone who is pregnant or planning to become pregnant.Please note: All treatments and relevant follow up must be performed at Michigan State University College of Veterinary Medicine. Investigational treatment will not be sent to outside clinics.

title: Immune treatment of Canine Bone Cancer
text: Dogs with bone cancer or osteosarcoma of the limbs will be first assessed with a specialized imaging called 18F-FDG PET-CT to determine that the tumor is limited to the leg.  Once enrolled, the dog will be treated with an immunotherapy directly in the tumor followed by chemotherapy the next 1-2 days prior to amputation.  The goal of this therapy is to increase the immune response to the tumor.  After amputation, treatment with standard chemotherapy will be augmented with an immune checkpoint inhibitor.  At three, six, and twelve months after amputation, non-invasive imaging will be performed to look for spread of osteosarcoma.  All treatments performed at the Center for Image-Guided Animal Therapy at Johns Hopkins in Baltimore, MD are free-of-charge.  The immune checkpoint inhibitor will be provided free-of-charge.  The owner will need to make arrangements for amputation and chemotherapy with a surgeon and medical oncologist, respectively.

title: Clinical trial for dogs newly diagnosed with osteosarcoma
text: In this study we will investigate the therapeutic potential of immune cells known as invariant natural killer T (iNKT) cells, made from the blood of a healthy donor dog, in dogs with bone cancer. iNKT cells are potent immune cells that have been shown to kill cancer cells in mouse models and in some human cancer patients. The iNKT cells directly kill the tumor (cancer cell) and  they also boost the patient's own anti-tumor (cancer-killing) immune responses. In this study, we will genetically modify these natural killer T cells (NKT) cells to express a protein known as a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR). The CAR directs the genetically modified CAR-iNKT cells to a target protein (known as B7H3) on the bone cancer cell. The CAR-iNKT cells kill the bone cancer cells and activate the immune system to do the same. The purpose of this study is to determine i) the safety of CAR-iNKT cells, ii) their ability to traffic to the bone tumor in your dog’s leg and exert an anti-cancer effect there, iii) their ability to delay or prevent metastatic disease and iv) how long the CAR-iNKT cells remain in your dog’s body. This clinical trial is fully funded and at no cost to owners. Covered procedures include:Bloodwork for general health screeningChest radiographs to be sure the osteosarcoma has not spread to the lungs prior to treatmentBone biopsy to confirm osteosarcoma and the presence of the B7H3 target proteinCellular therapy with iNKT cellsAmputation of the affected limb (~10 days after cell therapy) and all post-op care/hospitalizationStandard of care chemotherapyFollow up monitoring of bloodwork and chest radiographsAll clinical trial visits are in person at the University of Pennsylvania School of Veterinary Medicine in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.

title: Feasibility and dose-optimization clinical trial of local immunotherapy for solid tumors in canine cancer patients
text: WHY IS THIS STUDY BEING DONE?Immunotherapies are a class of anti-cancer treatments that work by activating a patient’s own immune system to fight specific diseases, including cancer. A number of immunotherapies have been approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for use in humans in a wide range of diseases, including cancer. While these therapies have shown positive results in cancers of blood cells, they have had more limited successes in solid tumors like soft tissue sarcoma. This is thought to be in part because it is hard to get enough of the drug into the tumor when it is given through the blood stream (intravenously) without causing serious side effects. To overcome this limitation, this research study will use injections of immunotherapies directly through the skin into the tumor (intra-tumoral injections). The primary goal of this research study is to test whether it is safe and feasible to treat tumors by injecting them with a certain type of immunotherapy called T-cell engagers (TCEs).  A T cell is a special kind of white blood cell that attacks sick cells in your body, including virus-infected cells and cancer cells. TCEs are a new kind of cancer immunotherapy that helps a patient’s own T cells find and kill cancer cells. They work like a connector: one end sticks to a cancer cell, and the other end sticks to a T cell. By pulling the two cells together, the TCE helps the T cell recognize the cancer cell and activate its killing response. In this research study, two different TCEs will be tested together (TCE combination). They work in much the same way, but each one attaches to different markers on cancer cells and T cells. Because they target different markers, the two treatments can help T cells kill cancer cells more effectively, even at lower doses of each TCE, which helps reduce the chance of harmful side effects. The goal is to make the therapy work better while still keeping patients safe.The study will test different doses of TCEs per injection, different numbers of injections placed into the tumor itself, and the product used to dilute the TCEs. The TCE combination will be diluted either in sterile saline (a solution of salt and water) or in hydrogel (a water-based gel). The hydrogel’s job is to slowly release the drugs into the tumor, with the goal to keep the cancer cells exposed to the drugs for a longer time. This may help the treatment work better and could also reduce side effects. The TCE combination will also be mixed with sterile fluorescent dye(s) that will help researchers track where the injections were placed in the tumor. The fluorescent dye(s) have already been used in multiple canine and human clinical trials with no known side effects.  The “investigational” part of the study are the intratumoral injections of the TCE combinations diluted in sterile saline or hydrogel. These TCEs are investigational drugs, which means they have not yet been approved by the FDA or the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) for use in dogs or other species. The purpose of this study is to test the safety and the biological effect of the TCE combination in canine patients with soft tissue sarcoma (STS), rather than to specifically provide medical treatment to the enrolled patient.

title: Enhanced Ethanol Ablation for Feline Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma
text: Some cancer patients have a poor prognosis, despite intensive multimodal therapy (e.g., surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy). In other cases, these treatments are likely to improve outcome but are inaccessible (e.g., financial, scheduling and/or geographical limitations). Thus, there is an immense need for treatments that offer effective tumor control and palliation, and that ideally can be given at low-cost in the primary care setting. We have recently demonstrated proof-of-concept for a low-cost effective option, called enhanced ethanol ablation. Ethanol ablation (intratumoral injectionof pure ethanol) was originally used for human liver cancer, achieving survival rates similar to surgical resection for small tumors. However, conventional ethanol ablation is ineffective for superficial, large, and/or poorly encapsulated lesions, and requires large injection volumes. Enhanced ethanol ablation involves controlled injection of an ethyl cellulose- ethanol mixture directly into the tumor. When mixed with ethyl cellulose, a water-insoluble ethanol-based gel is formed. We have shown this caused complete regression in 7 of 7 chemically-induced tumors in the hamster oral cavity while dramatically reducing the required injection volume. Now, we will perform a pilot study to evaluate safety and efficacy in feline oral squamous cell carcinomas, which serves as a model for other large, superficial and invasive tumors. Cats with oral squamous cell carcinoma (mandibular and maxillary) will be enrolled. They will have basic staging tests performed, and then undergo anesthesia for a intratumoral injection of ethyl cellulose-ethanol. The tumor will be imaged using CT, before and after injection. Cats will be hospitalized overnight for observation, after this first injection. They will then return for periodic recheck exams to evaluate for toxicity and changes in tumor size. Depending on response to the first injection, cats may be eligible for up to 2 booster injections. Cats will be dismissed from the study at the time of local disease progression, or after 6 months of follow-up.

title: Ethos Precision Medicine Umbrella Study for Hemangiosarcoma (Ethos-PUSH)
text: Canine splenic hemangiosarcoma is an aggressive cancer with limited treatment options available. Dogs presenting with this disease often have spontaneous internal bleeding that results in sudden onset of weakness or collapse. Although this is a common consequence for hemangiosarcoma, any other tumor of the spleen can spontaneously bleed resulting in these same changes. Dogs who have a bleeding splenic tumor must undergo surgery to remove the spleen (called splenectomy). This procedure both removes the source of life-threatening hemorrhage and provides tissue samples for making a final diagnosis. Roughly 40% of dogs have benign splenic disease causing the internal bleeding and will be cured with surgery alone. Many of the remaining dogs will have hemangiosarcoma as the cause of their bleeding and will require chemotherapy following surgery to delay or prevent metastatic disease. For dogs with splenic hemangiosarcoma, the combination of surgery and chemotherapy has been estimated to provide median survival times of 4-9 months with only a small percentage of dogs surviving to 2 years. Ethos-PUSH embarks on a journey to improve the outcome of canine hemangiosarcoma by furthering our understanding of this disease. Dogs confirmed to have hemangiosarcoma will be randomized to receive 1 of 4 treatments. These treatment groups include standard therapies and novel therapies that have been selected as potential targets against previously defined genomic alterations in hemangiosarcoma. Treatment arms will be compared to determine a best protocol, which will serve as the benchmark for future treatment studies. Furthermore, tumor and blood samples will be collected and serve as platforms for nationwide collaborations to improve the molecular understanding of this disease and match molecular biomarkers with treatment response to specific therapeutics. This comprehensive approach is designed to bring about curative outcomes for dogs suffering from this aggressive cancer. A 501(c)(3) nonprofit incubator of scientific innovation, Ethos Discovery has developed the most innovative scientific portfolio in the field of animal health and delivers answers to our clinical research questions through rigorous clinical trials made available to pet patients. The mission of Ethos Discovery is to improve health outcomes for humans and animals with complex medical problems. We are agnostic to the source of good ideas and uniquely positioned, with the support of Ethos Veterinary Health, to reach patients and doctors nationally and partner with key leaders in their field internationally. This flexibility provides us the opportunity to pursue impactful research that will make a difference where it is most important, at the point of care and for the benefit of patients and families in the community.

title: Vaccine Study for Dogs with Melanoma
text: Participation involves an initial staging visit and 5 follow up visits. The vaccine will be given 4 times approximately 4 weeks apart followed by 2 restaging visits. Booster vaccines will also be available 6 months after completion of the entire vaccine series at an additional charge.

title: Cell Therapy for Metastatic Osteosarcoma
text: In this study we will investigate the therapeutic potential of a type of white blood cell known as invariant natural killer T (iNKT) cells that are made from the blood of a healthy donor dog. iNKT cells are potent immune cells that kill cancer cells in mouse models and in some human cancer patients. In this study, we will use iNKT cells that express a cancer targeting receptor known as a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR). The CAR directs the modified iNKT cells to the cancer cells which are then killed. The CAR-iNKT cells also will further activate the patient's own immune system to help kill the cancer cells. The purpose of this study is to determine the safety of CAR-iNKT cells, their maximum tolerated dose, how long they will remain in the patient and their effectiveness against bone cancer that has spread to the lungs.

title: Evaluation of a combination of three drugs in dogs with hemangiosarcoma
text: The objective of this study is to investigate the effectiveness of combining doxorubicin or carboplatin and temozolomide with propranolol in dogs with hemangiosarcoma. The use of either doxorubicin or carboplatin alone as a treatment for hemangiosarcoma has been studied, and studies with propranolol (historically used to treat heart disease) have shown promise as an added treatment against hemangiosarcoma, however, survival times still remain quite low. We are hopeful that survival times can be further improved using a combination approach to treatment, with combination of both intravenous and oral treatments. Dogs with hemangiosarcoma of the spleen, liver, heart or intramuscular region will be considered for inclusion in this study.

title: Radiation + Targeted Therapy for Bladder Cancer in Dogs
text: Transitional cell carcinoma (TCC) is the most common form of bladder tumors in dogs. Fractionated radiation therapy is one of the most effective treatment options for this form of tumor, and is typically combined with chemotherapy and an NSAID medication. Lapatinib is a newer therapy that has been used as a single agent for the treatment of dogs with this form of bladder tumor. The goal of this trial is to see if the combination of radiation therapy and lapatinib will be safe and well tolerated in dogs with TCC. If your dog participates in this study, they will receive oral lapatinib through the course of the approximately 4-month study, as well as oral NSAIDs. 5-7 days after starting these medications, they will also complete 15 daily (M-F) fractions of radiation therapy, which requires daily general anesthesia. Patients will get a urinary ultrasound at the beginning and end of the study, which may require sedation for some patients. They will also receive routine bloodwork throughout the course of the study, as well as blood collection at the beginning of radiation, end of radiation, and the conclusion of the study for study purposes.

title: Targeted Radiopharmaceutical Therapy (RPT) in Companion Dogs with Peripheral T-Cell Lymphoma (PTCL)
text: In collaboration with the UW Carbone Cancer Center, we are developing an innovative treatment for canine Peripheral T-cell Lymphoma (PTCL). This study aims to evaluate the safety, effectiveness, and optimal dosage of ⁹⁰Y-NM600 targeted radiopharmaceutical therapy (RPT) in dogs with PTCL. Our research indicates that targeted RPT can effectively reach tumors, regardless of tumor location.Please note that this is not a double-masked trial; ALL enrolled patients will receive the targeted RPT.This funded study (after initial screening) covers the following expenses:All required examination visits EXCEPT for the initial screening visit.All laboratory work (CBC, blood chemistry, urinalysis), EXCLUDING the initial lab work needed for initial screening.Tumor BiopsyPET-CT scans.Hospitalization.All costs related to RPT.Additionally, up to $1,000 is available to help manage any treatment-related side effects, should they occur.Please be aware that there is no financial incentive for enrolling your pet in this trial. Dogs showing a positive response or stable disease at the day 21 assessment may be eligible for an additional 90Y-NM600 dose.Dogs with progressive disease will be withdrawn from the study and offered either standard of care chemotherapy (at the clients expense) or treatment discontinuation, based on the client's preference.Please note that the standard of care chemotherapy is NOT part of the trial.

title: Using a Fluorescent Dye to Identify Bladder Tumors in Dogs During Surgery
text: Urothelial carcinoma (UC) is the most common type of bladder cancer in dogs. For dogs with tumors in certain locations, surgical removal (partial cystectomy) can improve outcomes with low risk. New minimally invasive techniques that maintain a closed bladder may offer additional benefits and warrant further investigation, but these approaches currently rely on specialized camera equipment within the bladder, which is not always available, to identify tumors. This pilot study will test whether a safe dye, indocyanine green (ICG), used with near-infrared (NIR) imaging can identify bladder tumors and their edges during surgery. The findings with NIR will be compared with what is seen by the surgeon and with microscopic examination by a pathologist. Results will be incorporated into future studies with novel surgical techniques that have the potential to improve outcomes in dogs with UC.Dogs enrolled in the study will receive a single intravenous injection of ICG approximately 24 hours before their planned surgery for bladder tumor removal, and a special near-infrared camera will be used during the procedure to assess whether the tumor and its margins fluoresce differently than surrounding normal tissue. ICG is an FDA-approved dye that is commonly used for other imaging purposes in human and veterinary medicine, but its use for identifying bladder tumors during surgery in dogs is considered investigational and its effectiveness for this purpose has not yet been established. A total of five dogs will be enrolled in this study, and all dogs will receive the same dye injection and imaging procedure during their planned surgery; there are no separate treatment or control groups. Study participation is complete after surgery is performed.
